Newsletter issued whenever the market moves

lessons.title: Exempt from registration: federal and state
lessons.objective: Identify the federal exemptions and the USA's no-place-of-business, institutional, snowbird and de minimis exemptions.

blocks.b:
Two kinds of adviser meet the definition but need not register with the SEC:
1. **Intrastate advisers** — all clients are residents of the state where the adviser has its principal office and **only** place of business, **and** it gives **no advice on securities listed on a national exchange**. (Not available to advisers to private funds.)
2. Advisers whose **only clients are insurance companies**.

The exam loves to ask whether an adviser whose only clients are **banks** is exempt under federal law. **No** — that exemption exists under **state** law (institutional clients), not under the Advisers Act.

An adviser with **no place of business in the state** (registered in some other state) is exempt from registering there if its only clients in the state are:
- **broker-dealers**
- **other investment advisers**
- **institutional investors** — banks, trust companies, S&Ls, insurance companies, investment companies, **employee benefit plans with at least $1 million**, government agencies
- **existing clients who are not residents and are only temporarily in the state** (the **snowbird** exemption — no time limit on 'temporary', but if the client moves there legally the adviser has **30 days** to register or stop)
- **five or fewer** other (retail) clients resident in the state during the **preceding 12 months** (**de minimis**)
- anyone else the Administrator exempts.

**Retail client** = noninstitutional; an individual, trust or estate is always retail. 'Five or fewer' and 'fewer than six' are the same thing; a sixth retail client ends the exemption.

blocks.h: What counts as a 'place of business'?
blocks.b: Every state exemption above depends on having **no place of business** in the state. Advertising to the **public** that you will meet prospective clients at a hotel, country club or seminar in the state **creates** a place of business. Telling only **existing clients** you will be passing through and available in your hotel room does **not**. And once you have any place of business in a state, you must register there — even with a single client.

An adviser registered in State A, with no office anywhere else, advised **five** individuals in State B over 12 months → no State B registration. Six individuals → must register. Six banks, six insurers and six other IAs → still no registration, because every client is institutional.

lessons.title: Private fund, venture capital and foreign private advisers
lessons.objective: Identify the private fund adviser, venture capital and foreign private adviser exemptions, NASAA's version, and exempt reporting advisers.

blocks.b:
The **Private Fund Investment Advisers Registration Act of 2010** (Title IV of Dodd-Frank) created three exemptions from SEC registration:
- **Private fund adviser** — advises **only private funds** and has **less than $150 million** in U.S. AUM.
- **Foreign private adviser** — no U.S. place of business, **fewer than 15** U.S. clients and investors, **less than $25 million** attributable to them, and does not hold itself out in the U.S. or advise a registered fund.
- **Venture capital fund adviser** — advises only VC funds (limited leverage, no redemption rights, holds itself out as VC, not registered under the 1940 Act); **no AUM limit**.

These exemptions turn on **whom** you advise, not what securities you discuss.

A **private fund** is an issuer that would be an investment company but for **Section 3(c)(1)** or **3(c)(7)** of the Investment Company Act:
- **3(c)(1)**: **no more than 100** beneficial owners, all **accredited investors**, no public offering.
- **3(c)(7)**: owned only by **qualified purchasers** (**$5 million** in investments for individuals, generally **$25 million** for entities), no public offering, **no limit** on the number of investors.

Hedge fund managers generally register with the SEC even though the funds themselves do not.

Exempt private fund and VC advisers designated **exempt reporting advisers (ERAs)** still file, through **IARD**, certain items of **Form ADV Part 1** (public on the SEC site). ERAs **do not prepare Part 2**.

**Form PF** is different: it is filed by advisers **registered** with the SEC that manage private funds with **at least $150 million** in private fund AUM at fiscal year end.

The state version mirrors the federal exemption, except:
1. For a **3(c)(1)** fund, every investor must be a **qualified client**: at least **$1.1 million** in AUM with the adviser right after signing, or net worth (with spouse) the adviser reasonably believes exceeds **$2.2 million**, **excluding the primary residence** (net of debt secured by it). Note 'qualified client' is far less than 'qualified purchaser'.
2. Neither the adviser nor its affiliates may be **bad actors** (certain felonies, SEC orders, SRO expulsions).

blocks.h: Private fund vs. VC fund adviser

lessons.title: SEC or state? NSMIA, Dodd-Frank thresholds and the buffers
lessons.objective: Determine whether an adviser registers with the SEC or the states using the AUM thresholds, their exceptions, the buffers and the switching deadlines.

blocks.b:
Before 1996 advisers registered with the SEC **and** the states. **NSMIA** bifurcated it: an adviser registers with the **SEC or the state(s), never both**, by creating the **federal covered adviser**. The three most tested categories:
1. Registered with the SEC because **eligible ($100 million AUM)** or **required ($110 million)**.
2. Under contract to a **registered investment company** (a mutual fund) — **regardless of size**.
3. **Excluded** from the federal definition — most tested: advisers solely on **U.S. government securities**. Because federal law excludes them, states cannot define them as IAs.

- **Large — $100 million or more**: eligible for the SEC; at **$110 million** SEC registration is **mandatory**; states are preempted.
- **Small — under $25 million**: SEC registration **prohibited**, state registration required — unless it advises a registered investment company, or would have to register in **15 or more states** (then SEC is permitted).
- **Mid-size — $25 million to under $100 million**: generally state, but **not prohibited** from the SEC if (a) it is not required to register in its principal-office state, (b) it would not be subject to examination there, (c) it would need **15+ states**, or (d) it uses the buffer. 'Not prohibited' means *eligible*, not *required*.

Other SEC exceptions to the prohibition: **pension consultants** to plans with at least **$200 million** of assets; advisers expecting SEC eligibility within **120 days** of filing; **internet advisers**.

- **$10 million buffer**: a state-registered adviser may stay with the state from $100 million until it hits **$110 million**.
- **$20 million buffer**: once SEC-registered, it need not leave until AUM drops **below $90 million**.

AUM is measured **once a year on the annual updating amendment**, so mid-year swings don't force a switch. Three deadlines to memorize:
1. State IA reports **$110 million+** → register with the SEC within **90 days**.
2. New adviser expects **$100 million within 120 days** → may register with the SEC now.
3. SEC IA reports **under $90 million** → withdraw and register with the states within **180 days** (one agency is faster than many states, so the state move gets twice the time).

lessons.title: Form ADV and the registration process
lessons.objective: Describe the parts of Form ADV, IARD, control persons, amendments and renewal, notice filing, consent to service of process, effective dates and withdrawal.

blocks.b: To register with a state Administrator you **submit an application, provide a consent to service of process, pay filing fees, post a bond if required, and pass any exam the Administrator requires** (written, oral or both). The application is **Form ADV**, filed through the **IARD** (Investment Adviser Registration Depository) — the electronic system for registration, regulatory review and public disclosure.

blocks.h: The four parts of Form ADV
blocks.b:
- **Part 1A** — for regulators; **everyone** files it: principal office, location of books and records, form of organization, other business (BD, agent), custody/discretion, **control persons**, disciplinary history. Includes **Schedule A** (direct owners and executive officers) and **Disclosure Reporting Pages** (disciplinary events).
- **Part 1B** — extra state questions; **SEC registrants skip it**.
- **Part 2A** — the **brochure**: plain-English narrative for clients — fees, types of clients, investments, **strategies**, methods of analysis, education and background of those who advise, and an **audited balance sheet** if the adviser takes substantial prepayment of fees or (state-registered) has custody.
- **Part 2B** — **brochure supplements** about the supervised persons who give advice.

Mnemonic: **2A = Adviser, 2B = Bodies**. State registrants file Parts 1 and 2 with each state.

Under the Advisers Act and the USA, **25% or more** of voting securities (or partnership capital) is presumed control; officers, partners and directors are presumed to control. Compare: **more than 10%** under the Securities Exchange Act, and **more than 25%** under the Investment Company Act.

- **Annual updating amendment** within **90 days after fiscal year end** — verifies AUM and includes a summary of material changes to the brochure.
- **Prompt amendments** whenever these change: name, principal office, location of records, contact person, organizational structure, brochure accuracy, disciplinary answers, custody policy.
- Changing business form (sole proprietor → corporation) = new ADV, **no fee**.
- **Successor firm** files a new ADV: with the SEC, **pay a fee**; under the USA, **no additional fee**.
- **Notice filing**: federal covered advisers don't register with states but pay state fees and give notice (not needed if they deal only with institutions, BDs and IAs).

blocks.h: Consent to service, effective dates, renewal
blocks.b:
- **Consent to service of process** appoints the Administrator as attorney to receive noncriminal securities-related legal process; filed with the **initial** application and **permanent** — never renewed.
- Effective: **SEC — 45th day** after a complete filing; **state — noon of the 30th day**.
- Every state registration renews **December 31** — register in November and you still renew the next December 31.
- Passing the Series 65 gives **no right** to do business until the state grants registration; while pending, only clerical work or internal research is allowed.

Voluntary withdrawal is on **Form ADV-W**; it is held up if proceedings are pending.
- **SEC**: effective on acceptance by IARD, but registration continues **60 days** solely so a proceeding can be started.
- **State**: effective **30 days** after filing (the Administrator may shorten it), with jurisdiction retained for **one year**.

lessons.title: Financial requirements
lessons.objective: Apply the substantial prepayment thresholds, financial impairment disclosure, net worth and bonding rules, and the net worth deficiency procedure.

blocks.b: The Advisers Act sets **no minimum net worth**, but it does require disclosure. A **substantial prepayment of fees** is **more than $500 (USA)** or **more than $1,200 (federal)**, **six months or more in advance** — both parts must be true. Any adviser with **discretion**, **custody**, or **substantial prepayment** must disclose any financial condition reasonably likely to impair its ability to meet contractual commitments (for example, a large arbitration award).
$800 for the next **calendar quarter** is not substantial — under six months. $800 for the **contract year** is substantial under the USA (more than $500, six months or more).

The Administrator may require a **minimum net worth or surety bond**; custody is higher than discretion:
- **Discretion**: $10,000 net worth
- **Custody** (with or without discretion): $35,000 net worth
- **Bond in lieu of net worth**: $35,000 either way
- **Neither custody nor discretion, but substantial prepayment**: positive net worth at all times

A state-registered adviser that meets the requirements of the state of its **principal office** (the executive office from which officers direct and coordinate the firm) satisfies every other state — the same is true for recordkeeping. Under **NSMIA Section 222**, financial, bonding and recordkeeping rules for **federal covered** advisers are **solely federal**.

Terminology: advisers have **net worth** requirements; broker-dealers have **net capital**. If a question says 'net capital' for an IA, answer it as asked.
A custodial adviser finds its net worth is $23,000 on Monday. Notice by Tuesday's close; report by Wednesday's close. Deficiency $12,000 → bond of **$15,000**.

lessons.title: Books, records and supervision
lessons.objective: Recall the required books and records, retention periods and storage rules, and the supervision framework including the CCO and supervised persons.

blocks.b: The Advisers Act and NASAA's model recordkeeping rule require, among others: journals and ledgers; a **memorandum of each order**; bank records and reconciliations; bills; financial statements; **written communications** received and sent about advice, funds or orders (for a mailing to more than 10 persons you need not keep recipients' names, but a list's source must be noted); records of **discretionary accounts** and powers of attorney; **written agreements**; a file of every **advertisement** sent to two or more persons — with a memo of reasons if it recommends a specific security without stating them; **litigation and complaint** files; registration documents for the firm and its IARs; and **personal securities transactions** of the adviser and its advisory representatives — a deterrent to **scalping** (trading ahead of your own recommendation). Willful false statements or omissions in filed reports are unlawful.

- **Five years** from the end of the fiscal year of the last entry, **readily accessible**; the **first two years in the principal office**. After two years, electronic or microfilm storage is fine.
- **Articles, charters, minute books, stock certificate books**: in the principal office until **three years after the enterprise terminates**.
- Media: paper, micrographic or **electronic** — with procedures to safeguard against loss or alteration, limit access to authorized personnel and the Administrator, and ensure complete, true, legible reproductions, all indexed for retrieval. Records are subject to **surprise audit**.
- Federal covered advisers follow only the SEC's rules; state-registered advisers follow only their principal-office state.

If a question asks how long records must be kept, the answer is **five years**. Two years is only how long they must be in the office. Six years is a broker-dealer number from another rule — not here.

Every registered adviser must:
- adopt and implement **written policies and procedures** to prevent violations, including **physical security and cybersecurity** policies tailored to its size, services and locations;
- **review them annually**; and
- designate a **chief compliance officer (CCO)** with the seniority and authority to enforce them — the CCO is **named on Form ADV**.

Failure to supervise can bring suspension or revocation of the firm's registration.

A **supervised person** is any officer, partner, director, employee or other person who advises on the firm's behalf under its supervision — chiefly the **IAR**. Supervised persons who individually meet the three prongs do not register as IAs; the **firm** registers and they register as IARs under it. **Independent-contractor** planners licensed through an IA are its IARs, supervised like employees; their cards may show their own entity but must also name the registered IA.

A **person associated with an investment adviser** is similar but **excludes clerical or ministerial** employees; *supervised person* includes everyone.

questions.stem: Under the Uniform Securities Act, which of the following would NOT be included in the definition of 'person'?
options: A nonprofit charitable corporation
A political subdivision of a state
A professional sports league
An individual a court has declared mentally incompetent
questions.explanation: The three nonpersons are a minor, a deceased individual, and an individual declared mentally incompetent by a court. Corporations, governments and their subdivisions, and associations are all persons.
why: A corporation is a person.
A government or political subdivision is a person.
An association is a person — even a sports league.

questions.stem: A financial planner prepares comprehensive plans for clients at no charge. She is paid only through commissions on the insurance policies she sells to implement the plans. Under the three-prong test, the compensation prong is
options: not met, because no fee is charged for the plan.
met, because compensation may be indirect.
not met, because insurance is not a security.
met only if the commissions exceed $500 per client.
questions.explanation: Compensation is any economic benefit, direct or indirect. Commissions on products sold as part of the plan are compensation for the advice.
why: The absence of a separate fee does not matter when there is indirect compensation.
Whether insurance is a security concerns the advice prong, not compensation; the plan involves securities anyway.
There is no dollar threshold in the compensation prong.

questions.stem: A person giving advice, for compensation and as a regular business, on which of the following would be giving advice about securities?
options: Rare coins
Rental real estate
Mutual fund shares
Gold bullion
questions.explanation: Mutual fund shares are securities. Coins, real estate and precious metals are nonsecurities, so advice limited to them does not meet the first prong.
why: Collectibles are not securities.
Real estate is not a security.
Precious metals are not securities.

questions.stem: Which of the following advisers could properly describe itself as 'investment counsel'?
options: A planner who offers tax, estate and insurance planning along with investment advice
A publisher of a subscription service that signals when to buy and sell 100 listed stocks
A firm whose only business is managing client assets in model portfolios it monitors daily
A firm that performs a one-time asset allocation for each new client
questions.explanation: Investment counsel requires that advice be the principal business AND that the adviser provide continuous and regular supervisory or management services. Daily-monitored model portfolios meet both.
why: Advice is only one of a wide range of services, so it is not the principal business.
Market timing signals without ongoing account management are not supervisory services.
A one-time allocation without continuous monitoring is not supervisory service.

questions.stem: Under SEC Release IA-1092, which of the following is MOST likely to be an investment adviser?
options: A consultant who helps employee benefit plans select and evaluate their portfolio managers
A sports agent who negotiates a player's contract for 10% of salary
A person who manages collections of investment-grade stamps
A person who sells long-term care insurance
questions.explanation: IA-1092 specifically treats pension consultants advising plans on the selection, performance and retention of investment managers as investment advisers.
why: Negotiating a contract is not advice about securities; advising the player on securities would be.
Stamps are collectibles, not securities.
Selling insurance without a securities aspect is not investment advice.

questions.stem: SEC Release IA-1092 is best described as
options: a rule that exempted financial planners from the Investment Advisers Act.
an interpretation that extended the investment adviser definition to financial planners, pension consultants and sports or entertainment representatives.
the statute that created the federal covered adviser.
a rule establishing the $110 million SEC registration threshold.
questions.explanation: IA-1092 (1987) interprets the definition to include those who offer advice as part of a broader financial practice; much of it restated the three prongs, but its impact was expanding whom the definition reaches.
why: It brought planners in, not out.
The federal covered adviser came from NSMIA (1996).
AUM thresholds come from Dodd-Frank (2010).

questions.stem: An investment adviser that is EXEMPT from registration under the Uniform Securities Act
options: is not defined as an investment adviser.
meets the definition of investment adviser but is not required to register.
is not subject to the act's antifraud provisions.
must still file Form ADV Part 2 with the Administrator.
questions.explanation: Exemption means the person is an investment adviser by definition but is relieved of the registration requirement. Exclusion is what removes a person from the definition.
why: That describes an exclusion.
Antifraud provisions apply to everyone, exempt or excluded.
An exempt adviser does not register, so it does not file Part 2 with the state.

questions.stem: Who of the following would NOT need to seek an exemption from registration under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940?
options: An adviser whose only clients are insurance companies
An adviser solely to venture capital funds
An accountant whose advice is incidental to her practice and who charges no separate fee
An adviser with its only office in one state, in-state clients only, giving no advice on exchange-listed securities
questions.explanation: The accountant is excluded from the definition, so she is not an investment adviser and has no reason to look for an exemption. The other three meet the definition and rely on exemptions.
why: Exempt (insurance-company-only clients) — but still defined as an IA.
Exempt under the venture capital exemption — still an IA.
This is the intrastate exemption — still an IA.

questions.stem: The Uniform Securities Act excludes certain professionals whose advice is solely incidental to their practice. The exclusion applies to all of the following EXCEPT
options: a civil engineer.
an economist.
a college professor.
an accountant.
questions.explanation: The L.A.T.E. exclusion covers lawyers, accountants, teachers and engineers. Economists are not on the list.
why: Any professional engineer is covered.
A teacher is covered.
An accountant is covered.

questions.stem: A broker-dealer offers a program in which clients pay a single annual fee covering both portfolio advice and all trade executions. With respect to the definition of investment adviser, the broker-dealer
options: remains excluded because advice is incidental to brokerage.
loses the exclusion because the wrap fee is special compensation for advice.
remains excluded as long as the fee is under $1,200 per year.
is excluded only if it is also a bank holding company.
questions.explanation: The broker-dealer exclusion requires advice solely incidental to brokerage AND no special compensation. A wrap fee program (advisory plus execution for one fee) is special compensation, so the exclusion is lost.
why: A wrap fee program is not incidental advice.
There is no dollar threshold in the exclusion.
Bank status is a separate exclusion unrelated to wrap programs.

questions.stem: A newsletter sold by subscription provides securities recommendations. Instead of a regular schedule, issues are released whenever a significant market event occurs. Under the Uniform Securities Act, the publisher
options: is excluded from the definition of investment adviser as a bona fide publication.
is excluded because the advice is impersonal.
does not qualify for the publisher's exclusion because the publication is not of regular circulation.
is excluded only if the subscription fee is under $500.
questions.explanation: The publisher's exclusion requires a publication that is general and impersonal, bona fide, and of general and REGULAR circulation — not timed to market events. Episodic issues lose the exclusion.
why: Timing to market events defeats 'regular circulation'.
Impersonal content alone is not enough; all three criteria must be met.
Fee size is irrelevant to the exclusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is excluded from the definition of investment adviser under BOTH the Uniform Securities Act and the Investment Advisers Act of 1940?
options: A savings and loan association
A credit union
A savings institution
An adviser whose advice is limited to U.S. government securities
questions.explanation: For the bank exclusion, 'bank' includes a savings institution but not a savings and loan association, credit union or foreign bank. The U.S.-government-securities exclusion exists only under federal law.
why: S&Ls are specifically not 'banks' for this exclusion.
Credit unions do not get the bank exclusion.
That exclusion is in the federal act only, not the USA.

questions.stem: Under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, an adviser is exempt from SEC registration if its only clients are
options: banks.
insurance companies.
broker-dealers.
employee benefit plans with at least $1 million in assets.
questions.explanation: The federal exemptions are the intrastate adviser and the adviser whose only clients are insurance companies. Banks, broker-dealers and large plans support a STATE exemption, not a federal one.
why: Only-banks clients is a state-law exemption; the exam tests this trap.
Only-BD clients supports the state no-place-of-business exemption.
Large plans are institutional clients under state law only.

questions.stem: An adviser has its only office in Texas and all of its clients are Texas residents. It regularly recommends stocks listed on the NYSE. Under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, the adviser
options: qualifies for the intrastate exemption.
does not qualify for the intrastate exemption because it advises on exchange-listed securities.
is excluded from the definition as a state-registered adviser.
must register with the SEC only if its AUM exceeds $25 million.
questions.explanation: The intrastate exemption requires in-state clients, a single in-state place of business AND no advice on securities listed on a national exchange. Recommending NYSE stocks breaks it.
why: Advice on listed securities disqualifies the exemption.
State registration is not an exclusion from the federal definition.
Whether it must or may register with the SEC depends on AUM thresholds; the question is about the exemption.

questions.stem: A state-registered investment adviser would NOT qualify for the de minimis exemption in a state where it has no place of business if, during the preceding 12 months, it had
options: five retail clients resident in the state.
fewer than six retail clients resident in the state.
six or fewer retail clients resident in the state.
five or fewer retail clients resident in the state.
questions.explanation: De minimis allows five or fewer retail clients in the state in the preceding 12 months. 'Six or fewer' includes six, which is over the limit.
why: Five is within the limit.
'Fewer than six' means five or fewer — within the limit.
This is exactly the limit.

questions.stem: Bluff Advisers is registered in State A and has no office in State B. Over the past 12 months its only State B clients were four banks, three insurance companies and two other investment advisers. In State B, Bluff
options: must register because it has more than five clients in the state.
must register because insurance companies are retail clients.
need not register because all of its State B clients are institutions or other advisers.
must register within 30 days of its first State B client.
questions.explanation: With no place of business in the state, an adviser whose only in-state clients are broker-dealers, other advisers or institutional investors is exempt regardless of how many such clients it has. The five-client limit applies only to retail clients.
why: The count limit applies to retail clients; institutions are unlimited.
Insurance companies are institutional investors.
The 30-day rule concerns a snowbird client who becomes a resident.

questions.stem: An IAR registered in State M, with no office elsewhere, runs an advertisement in a State N newspaper inviting the public to meet him at a State N hotel to discuss their portfolios. As a result, under the Uniform Securities Act, the adviser
options: is considered to have a place of business in State N.
keeps the de minimis exemption as long as fewer than six people attend.
needs no registration because the meeting is temporary.
is exempt because hotels are not offices.
questions.explanation: Advertising to the public the availability of meeting prospective clients at a hotel, club, seminar or other location in the state creates a place of business there, ending the no-place-of-business exemptions. Notifying only existing clients that you will be passing through does not.
why: Once there is a place of business, the de minimis exemption is unavailable.
The temporary nature of the meeting does not matter when it is advertised to the public.
A hotel used for advertised public meetings is a place of business.

questions.stem: A client of a State A adviser spends every winter in State B, where the adviser has no office. This year the client sells her State A home and becomes a legal resident of State B. Assuming the de minimis exemption is unavailable, the adviser must
options: stop advising her immediately.
register in State B or stop doing business with her within 30 days.
register in State B within 90 days.
do nothing, because the snowbird exemption has no time limit.
questions.explanation: The snowbird exemption covers existing nonresident clients temporarily in the state. When the client changes legal residence, the adviser has 30 days to register in that state or discontinue business with her.
why: There is a 30-day grace period.
The period is 30 days, not 90 (90 days is the AUM switching deadline).
'No time limit' applies to temporary stays, not to a change of residence.

questions.stem: Under the Dodd-Frank Act, an adviser solely to private funds is exempt from SEC registration if its U.S. assets under management are less than
options: $25 million.
$100 million.
$150 million.
$200 million.
questions.explanation: The private fund adviser exemption applies to advisers solely to private funds with less than $150 million in U.S. AUM, regardless of the number or type of funds.
why: $25 million is the foreign private adviser AUM limit (and the small adviser line).
$100 million is the SEC eligibility threshold.
$200 million is the pension consultant plan-asset figure.

questions.stem: A private fund relying on Section 3(c)(1) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 may have no more than
options: 35 investors.
100 investors.
500 investors.
an unlimited number of investors, all of whom are qualified purchasers.
questions.explanation: A 3(c)(1) fund is limited to 100 beneficial owners (accredited investors) and no public offering. A 3(c)(7) fund has no numerical limit but requires qualified purchasers.
why: 35 is the nonaccredited investor limit in a Reg D private placement.
500 is not a private fund limit.
That describes 3(c)(7).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about exempt reporting advisers (ERAs) is TRUE?
options: ERAs file nothing with the SEC because they are exempt from registration.
ERAs must file Form PF regardless of size.
ERAs file certain items of Form ADV Part 1 through IARD but do not prepare Part 2.
ERAs must deliver a brochure to every investor annually.
questions.explanation: Although exempt from registration, ERAs electronically file reports on certain items of Form ADV Part 1 through IARD (made public), and they do not prepare Part 2. Form PF is filed by SEC-registered advisers with at least $150 million in private fund AUM.
why: ERAs do report, on Part 1 items.
Form PF is for registered advisers with $150 million or more in private fund assets.
No Part 2 brochure is required of an ERA.

questions.stem: Under NASAA's model rule exempting advisers to private funds, an investor in a 3(c)(1) fund must be a qualified client, meaning the investor has
options: at least $1.1 million managed by the adviser, or a net worth over $2.2 million excluding the primary residence.
at least $5 million in investments.
a net worth of $1 million including the primary residence.
income of $200,000 in each of the last two years.
questions.explanation: NASAA requires qualified clients in a 3(c)(1) fund: $1.1 million in AUM with the adviser immediately after contracting, or net worth (with spouse) the adviser reasonably believes exceeds $2.2 million, excluding the primary residence.
why: $5 million in investments is the qualified purchaser test for 3(c)(7).
Accredited investor net worth excludes the residence and is $1 million — not the qualified client test.
That is part of the accredited investor income test.

questions.stem: The venture capital fund adviser exemption differs from the private fund adviser exemption in that the venture capital exemption
options: allows advice to registered investment companies.
has no limit on assets under management.
is available only under state law.
requires at least 15 U.S. clients.
questions.explanation: Advisers solely to venture capital funds are exempt with unlimited AUM, whereas the private fund adviser exemption caps U.S. AUM below $150 million. Both are limited to private funds and neither requires SEC registration.
why: Both exemptions are limited to private funds.
Both exist under federal law (and NASAA's rule parallels them).
The 'fewer than 15 clients' figure belongs to the foreign private adviser definition.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be a federal covered investment adviser?
options: An adviser with $40 million in AUM registered in two states
The adviser under contract to a registered open-end investment company with $18 million in assets
An adviser with $90 million in AUM that has never registered with the SEC
A pension consultant to plans with $150 million in assets
questions.explanation: An adviser to an investment company registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 is federal covered and registers with the SEC regardless of the amount of assets.
why: A $40 million adviser is mid-size and state-registered.
$90 million is below the $100 million eligibility line for an adviser not already SEC-registered.
The pension consultant exception requires $200 million of plan assets.

questions.stem: The National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996 (NSMIA)
options: required all investment advisers to register with both the SEC and the states.
provided that investment advisers register with either the SEC or the states, but not both.
set the $150 million private fund adviser exemption.
created the exempt reporting adviser.
questions.explanation: NSMIA bifurcated registration by creating the federal covered adviser: an adviser registers with the SEC or the state(s), never both.
why: That was the situation BEFORE NSMIA.
The private fund exemption came from Dodd-Frank (2010).
ERAs also come from Dodd-Frank.

questions.stem: In the absence of any other exemption, registration with the SEC would be PROHIBITED for which of the following investment advisers?
options: An adviser that would otherwise be required to register in 17 states
An adviser with $103 million in assets under management
A pension consultant to employee benefit plans with $150 million in assets
The adviser to a registered mutual fund with $18 million in assets
questions.explanation: Pension consultants may register with the SEC only if the plans they advise have at least $200 million of assets. The 15-or-more-states exception, the $100–110 million buffer, and the investment company adviser rule all permit SEC registration.
why: 15 or more states lifts the prohibition.
Between $100 million and $110 million the adviser may choose the SEC.
Investment company advisers register with the SEC at any size.

questions.stem: A mid-size adviser is one with assets under management of
options: less than $25 million.
at least $25 million but less than $100 million.
at least $100 million but less than $110 million.
$110 million or more.
questions.explanation: Dodd-Frank defines small advisers as under $25 million, mid-size as $25 million to under $100 million, and large as $100 million or more.
why: Under $25 million is a small adviser.
$100–110 million is the large-adviser buffer zone.
$110 million or more requires SEC registration.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the circumstances under which a mid-size adviser is permitted to register with the SEC?
options: It is not required to register with the Administrator of the state where it keeps its principal office.
If registered, it would not be subject to examination by that Administrator.
It would be required to register in 15 or more states.
It manages at least $50 million for institutional clients.
questions.explanation: The mid-size exceptions are: not required to register in the principal-office state; not subject to examination there; required to register in 15 or more states; or electing the $100–110 million buffer. The type of client has nothing to do with it.
why: This is one of the listed exceptions.
This is one of the listed exceptions.
This is one of the listed exceptions.

questions.stem: A state-registered investment adviser reports $112 million in assets under management on its annual updating amendment. It must
options: register with the SEC within 90 days.
register with the SEC within 180 days.
remain state-registered until AUM reaches $120 million.
register with the SEC within 120 days.
questions.explanation: Once the annual update shows $110 million or more, SEC registration is mandatory and must be completed within 90 days. Switching from the SEC to the states (under $90 million) gets 180 days.
why: 180 days is the deadline for moving from the SEC to the states.
The mandatory line is $110 million, not $120 million.
120 days relates to a new adviser expecting to reach $100 million.

questions.stem: An SEC-registered adviser's AUM fell to $84 million in March but recovered to $95 million by the time it filed its annual updating amendment. The adviser
options: must withdraw from the SEC and register with the states within 180 days.
may remain SEC-registered because AUM is measured on the annual updating amendment and was at least $90 million.
must withdraw from the SEC because AUM fell below $100 million during the year.
must register with both the SEC and the states until AUM exceeds $110 million.
questions.explanation: AUM is measured once a year on the annual updating amendment. A federal covered adviser need not withdraw unless the reported AUM is below $90 million, and here it was $95 million.
why: Withdrawal is required only when the annual update shows under $90 million.
Intra-year dips do not matter, and the withdrawal line is $90 million, not $100 million.
An adviser never registers with both.

questions.stem: A newly formed investment adviser currently has $5 million under management but reasonably expects to have $100 million within four months. It
options: must register with the states until it actually reaches $100 million.
is eligible to register with the SEC because it expects eligibility within 120 days of filing Form ADV.
must register with the SEC immediately because expected AUM exceeds $110 million.
is prohibited from registering anywhere until it reaches $25 million.
questions.explanation: An adviser that expects to be eligible for SEC registration within 120 days of filing may register with the SEC from the start — common when a large broker-dealer launches an advisory affiliate.
why: The 120-day expectation exception avoids a short period of state registration.
It is eligible, not required; and there is no immediate requirement based on expectations.
Small advisers register with the states; there is no prohibition on registering.

questions.stem: A prospective client wants to know an investment adviser's methods of analysis and the types of investment strategies it uses. That information is found in
options: Form ADV Part 1A.
Form ADV Part 1B.
Form ADV Part 2A.
Form ADV Part 2B.
questions.explanation: Part 2A is the narrative brochure containing client-focused information: fees, types of clients, investments, strategies, methods of analysis, and backgrounds of those who render advice.
why: Part 1A is regulator-focused information about the firm.
Part 1B is extra questions for state registrants only.
Part 2B is the supplement about the individuals who give advice.

questions.stem: Which part of Form ADV is NOT completed by an adviser registering with the SEC?
options: Part 1A
Part 1B
Part 2A
Part 2B
questions.explanation: Part 1B asks additional questions required by state securities authorities. Advisers registering with the SEC do not complete it; Parts 1A, 2A and 2B apply to both SEC and state registrants.
why: Everyone files Part 1A.
Everyone prepares the brochure.
Everyone prepares brochure supplements.

questions.stem: Under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and NASAA's model rule, a person is presumed to control an investment adviser organized as a corporation if the person has the right to vote
options: more than 10% of a class of voting securities.
25% or more of a class of voting securities.
more than 25% of a class of voting securities.
more than 50% of a class of voting securities.
questions.explanation: Control for an IA is presumed at 25% or more (voting securities for a corporation; capital for a partnership). Compare: more than 10% under the Securities Exchange Act and more than 25% under the Investment Company Act.
why: More than 10% is the Exchange Act control person test.
More than 25% is the Investment Company Act test.
Majority ownership is not the test.

questions.stem: An investment adviser must file its annual updating amendment to Form ADV within
options: 30 days after the end of the calendar year.
60 days after the end of its fiscal year.
90 days after the end of its fiscal year.
120 days after the end of its fiscal year.
questions.explanation: The annual updating amendment is due within 90 days after the end of the adviser's fiscal year and updates all items, including the AUM used to confirm SEC or state eligibility.
why: The deadline keys off the fiscal year, and it is 90 days.
60 days is the SEC ADV-W jurisdiction tail.
120 days is the new-adviser SEC eligibility expectation window.

questions.stem: In which of the following cases must a NEW Form ADV be filed rather than an amendment?
options: The firm changes its fee schedule.
The firm relocates its principal office.
A successor firm takes over the business.
The firm adds a disciplinary disclosure.
questions.explanation: A successor firm registers by filing a new application (ADV Parts 1 and 2) — paying a fee with the SEC, no additional fee under the USA. The other changes are handled by amendment.
why: A brochure inaccuracy is corrected by amendment.
A change in principal office is a prompt amendment.
Disciplinary changes are amendments.

questions.stem: The consent to service of process filed by an investment adviser applicant
options: must be renewed each December 31 along with the registration.
appoints the Administrator as attorney to receive noncriminal securities-related legal process and remains in force permanently.
is required only of federal covered advisers that notice file.
expires one year after the adviser withdraws its registration.
questions.explanation: The consent to service of process is submitted with the initial application and remains in force permanently; it need not be resubmitted with renewals.
why: It is never renewed.
Every new applicant for state registration provides one.
The one-year period is the Administrator's post-withdrawal jurisdiction, not the consent's life.

questions.stem: An investment adviser's state registration became effective on November 15. Its registration first comes up for renewal on
options: the following November 15.
December 31 of the same year.
December 31 of the following year.
the 45th day after the next annual updating amendment.
questions.explanation: All registrations of securities professionals renew on December 31. A registration granted in November still renews the next December 31, making the first year a short one.
why: Renewal is not on the anniversary.
Renewal is the NEXT December 31, only weeks away.
The 45th day is the SEC effective-date rule for new registrations.

questions.stem: After a state-registered investment adviser files Form ADV-W, the Administrator retains jurisdiction over the former registrant for
options: 30 days.
60 days.
one year.
five years.
questions.explanation: State withdrawal is effective 30 days after filing (the Administrator may shorten it), but the Administrator retains jurisdiction for one year. For an SEC-registered adviser, withdrawal is effective on acceptance but registration continues 60 days solely to commence a proceeding.
why: 30 days is when the withdrawal becomes effective.
60 days is the SEC's post-withdrawal tail.
Five years is the records retention period.

questions.stem: Which of the following would NASAA consider a substantial prepayment of fees?
options: $500 covering the next six months
$800 covering the entire contract year
$800 covering the next calendar quarter
$5,000 covering the next month
questions.explanation: Under the USA a substantial prepayment is MORE than $500, six months or more in advance. $800 for a year satisfies both conditions.
why: $500 is not MORE than $500.
A quarter is less than six months.
One month is less than six months.

questions.stem: Mammon Money Managers has its principal office in State A and is also registered in States B, C and D. It exercises discretion over client accounts. Mammon must meet the net worth or bonding requirements of
options: the SEC.
State A only.
the state with the highest requirement.
each state in which it is registered.
questions.explanation: A state-registered adviser that meets the net worth or bonding requirements of the state where its principal office is located satisfies every other state in which it is registered.
why: SEC requirements do not apply to a state-registered firm.
The home state controls, whatever other states require.
Only the principal-office state's requirement must be met.

questions.stem: Under the NASAA model rule, a state-registered investment adviser that maintains custody of client funds but does NOT exercise discretion is typically required to maintain a minimum net worth of
options: a positive amount at all times.
questions.explanation: Custody requires $35,000 net worth whether or not discretion is exercised; discretion alone requires $10,000; substantial prepayment alone requires positive net worth. A surety bond in lieu is $35,000 in either case.
why: $10,000 applies to discretion without custody.
$50,000 is not a NASAA IA figure.
Positive net worth is the rule for an adviser with only substantial prepayment.

questions.stem: Defalcator Investment Advisers (DIA) is registered in States A, K and R. Disclosure of financial impairment is required in all of the following circumstances EXCEPT
options: DIA maintains custody of customer funds and securities.
DIA requires a quarterly prepayment of fees of $800.
DIA requires an annual prepayment of fees of $600.
DIA exercises discretion over customer advisory accounts.
questions.explanation: Disclosure is required when the adviser has custody, discretion, or substantial prepayment (USA: more than $500, six or more months in advance). $800 for a quarter fails the six-month test; $600 for a year qualifies.
why: Custody triggers the disclosure.
$600 for a year is more than $500 for six months or more.
Discretion triggers the disclosure.

questions.stem: A state-registered adviser with custody of client assets discovers that its net worth is $23,000 against a $35,000 requirement. The surety bond it must obtain is
questions.explanation: The bond equals the net worth deficiency rounded up to the nearest $5,000. $35,000 − $23,000 = $12,000, which rounds up to $15,000.
questions.calc: $35,000 required − $23,000 actual = $12,000 deficiency → round up to nearest $5,000 = $15,000
why: Rounding goes up, not down.
The deficiency must be rounded up to a $5,000 multiple.
$35,000 is the full bond-in-lieu amount, not the deficiency bond.

questions.stem: A state-registered investment adviser discovers on Monday that its net worth is below the required minimum. Under the Uniform Securities Act it must
options: notify the Administrator by close of business Tuesday and file a financial report, including the number of client accounts, by close of business Wednesday.
file a financial report by close of business Monday and notify the Administrator within 30 days.
notify the SEC by close of business Tuesday.
cease all advisory activity until net worth is restored.
questions.explanation: Notice to the Administrator of the principal-office state is due by close of business the next business day; a financial report (including the number of client accounts) is due by close of business the business day after that, along with a bond for the deficiency rounded up to $5,000.
why: The sequence is notice first (next business day), report the day after.
A state-registered adviser deals with the Administrator, not the SEC.
The rule requires notice, a report and a bond, not a shutdown.

questions.stem: Under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and the NASAA model rule, an investment adviser's books and records must be preserved for
options: two years from the end of the fiscal year of the last entry.
three years from the date of the last entry.
five years from the end of the fiscal year of the last entry, the first two in the principal office.
six years, the first two in an easily accessible place.
questions.explanation: Records are kept in a readily accessible place for five years from the end of the fiscal year during which the last entry was made, the first two years in the adviser's principal office.
why: Two years is only the in-office portion.
Three years applies to organizational documents after the business terminates.
Six years is not the IA retention period.

questions.stem: An adviser registered in State G must keep certain books and records. Which of the following statements is NOT true?
options: Records originally created on a computer may be stored electronically.
Records are subject to surprise audit by the State G Administrator.
Written records may be reduced to microfilm.
Records must be kept for six years.
questions.explanation: The retention period is five years. Electronic and micrographic storage are permitted with safeguards, and records are subject to surprise examination.
why: Electronic storage is permitted with procedures to safeguard and reproduce the records.
The Administrator may examine records at any time.
Micrographic media are permitted.

questions.stem: The requirement that advisory representatives report their personal securities transactions to the adviser is designed primarily to deter
options: churning.
scalping.
front running by broker-dealers.
selling away.
questions.explanation: Scalping is trading on the anticipated short-run market effect of a recommendation before it is disseminated. The recordkeeping rule's requirement that all advisory representatives report their securities transactions, subject to SEC examination, serves as a deterrent.
why: Churning is excessive trading in a client's account to generate commissions.
Front running is a broker-dealer trading ahead of a customer order; this rule targets advisory personnel.
Selling away is an agent transacting outside the firm's supervision.

questions.stem: Amir owns Best Financial Planning, Inc. (BFPI) and is licensed as an investment adviser representative of Fortune Awaits You (FAY), an adviser registered in several states. Responsibility for supervising Amir's advisory activity rests with
options: Amir, as sole proprietor of BFPI.
BFPI.
FAY.
the Administrator of the state where BFPI has its principal office.
questions.explanation: Independent financial planners licensed as IARs of an advisory firm are supervised by that firm, just like employees. The registered adviser is responsible for its IARs' actions.
why: An IAR cannot supervise himself.
BFPI is not the registered adviser.
The Administrator regulates but does not supervise an adviser's representatives.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about an investment adviser's compliance program is TRUE?
options: The chief compliance officer's identity is kept confidential and not disclosed to regulators.
Written policies must be reviewed at least annually, and a chief compliance officer must be designated and disclosed on Form ADV.
A supervised person excludes clerical employees, while an associated person includes them.
Cybersecurity policies are required only of federal covered advisers.
questions.explanation: Every registered adviser must adopt written policies and procedures, review them annually, and designate a CCO whose identity is disclosed on Form ADV. Supervised person includes all employees; associated person excludes clerical staff. Cybersecurity policies are required of advisers generally.
why: The CCO must be disclosed on Form ADV.
It is the reverse: supervised person includes clerical staff; associated person excludes them.
Physical security and cybersecurity policies are required of investment advisers, not only federal covered ones.

questions.front: The three NONpersons under the USA
questions.back: A minor, a deceased individual, and an individual a court has declared mentally incompetent. Everything else (corporations, governments, associations, trusts) is a person.

questions.front: Three-prong test for an investment adviser
questions.back: (1) Advice about securities (even indirect; not commodities, collectibles, metals, real estate); (2) in the business — regularity or holding out; (3) compensation — any economic benefit, direct or indirect.

questions.front: Two criteria to use the term 'investment counsel'
questions.back: Principal business is giving investment advice, AND the adviser provides investment supervisory services (continuous and regular supervision/management of accounts).

questions.front: Who did SEC Release IA-1092 (1987) bring into the IA definition?
questions.back: Financial planners, pension consultants (funding advice or selecting/monitoring managers), and sports/entertainment representatives who give investing, tax, budgeting or money-management advice.

questions.front: Exclusion vs. exemption; federal covered adviser
questions.back: Exclusion = not in the definition (only antifraud applies). Exemption = defined as an IA but not required to register. Federal covered adviser (NSMIA 1996) = SEC-only, excluded from the USA definition.

questions.front: The exclusions from the IA definition
questions.back: USA: banks/BHCs/savings institutions/trust companies (not credit unions, S&Ls, foreign banks); L.A.T.E. (solely incidental, no separate fee); BDs with no special compensation (wrap fee loses it); bona fide regular publishers; IARs; federal covered advisers; Administrator-specified. Federal adds: advice only on U.S. government securities.

(1) Intrastate adviser — all clients in the state of its only office, no advice on exchange-listed securities, not a private fund adviser; (2) only clients are insurance companies. Only-banks is a STATE exemption, not federal.

questions.front: USA exemption for an adviser with no place of business in the state
questions.back: Only clients in the state are BDs, other IAs, institutions (incl. benefit plans ≥ $1M), snowbirds (existing nonresident clients temporarily there; 30 days to register if they move), or ≤ 5 retail clients in the preceding 12 months (de minimis). Advertising public meetings in the state creates a place of business.

questions.front: Private fund adviser exemption; 3(c)(1) vs 3(c)(7); ERA; Form PF
questions.back: Exempt if solely private funds and < $150M U.S. AUM. 3(c)(1): ≤ 100 accredited investors. 3(c)(7): qualified purchasers ($5M individuals / $25M entities), no limit. ERAs file ADV Part 1 items via IARD, no Part 2. Form PF: SEC-registered advisers with ≥ $150M private fund AUM.

questions.front: NASAA qualified client; foreign private adviser; VC adviser
questions.back: Qualified client: $1.1M AUM with adviser or $2.2M net worth excluding primary residence; no bad actors. Foreign private adviser: no U.S. office, < 15 U.S. clients/investors, < $25M U.S. AUM, no holding out. VC fund adviser: exempt with unlimited AUM.

questions.front: Three most-tested categories of federal covered adviser
questions.back: (1) SEC-registered because eligible ($100M) or required ($110M); (2) adviser to a registered investment company — any size; (3) excluded from the federal definition, e.g., advice only on U.S. government securities.

Small < $25M: state. Mid-size $25M–< $100M: state unless not required to register/not examined in home state, 15+ states, or buffer. Large ≥ $100M: SEC eligible; ≥ $110M required. Also SEC-permitted: investment company advisers (any size), pension consultants to ≥ $200M of plans, 120-day expectation, internet advisers.

$10M buffer: stay state-registered from $100M until $110M. $20M buffer: stay SEC-registered until below $90M. Measured on the annual updating amendment. ≥ $110M → SEC within 90 days. < $90M → states within 180 days. Expect $100M within 120 days → may register with SEC now.

1A: firm info for regulators (everyone; Schedule A owners, DRPs). 1B: state-only questions. 2A: brochure (fees, clients, strategies, backgrounds; audited balance sheet if substantial prepayment or state custody). 2B: supplements on advising persons. Control: 25%+ (Advisers Act/USA) vs > 10% (Exchange Act) vs > 25% (Investment Company Act).

questions.front: ADV updating, effective dates, renewal, consent to service, ADV-W
questions.back: Annual updating amendment within 90 days of fiscal year end; prompt amendments for material changes; successor firm = new ADV (SEC fee / USA no fee). Effective: SEC 45th day; state noon of 30th day. Renewal every Dec 31. Consent to service of process is permanent. ADV-W: SEC effective on acceptance + 60-day tail; state effective in 30 days, 1-year jurisdiction.

questions.front: Substantial prepayment; net worth and bonding
questions.back: Substantial prepayment: > $500 (USA) / > $1,200 (federal), 6+ months in advance. Financial impairment disclosure if discretion, custody or substantial prepayment. Net worth: discretion $10,000; custody $35,000; bond in lieu $35,000; prepayment only → positive net worth. Home-state (principal office) requirements suffice; federal covered advisers follow SEC only.

Notify the Administrator by close of business the next business day; file a financial report (including number of client accounts) by close of business the following business day; obtain a bond for the deficiency rounded UP to the nearest $5,000. Net worth excludes goodwill/intangibles, personal home/furnishings/cars, loans to officers/partners.

Five years from the end of the fiscal year of the last entry, readily accessible; first two years in the principal office. Organizational documents: three years after termination. Paper, microfilm or electronic storage allowed with safeguards. Personal trade records deter scalping. Federal covered → SEC rules; state-registered → home-state rules.

questions.front: Supervision requirements; supervised vs. associated person
questions.back: Written policies and procedures (incl. cybersecurity), annual review, CCO named on Form ADV. Supervised person = officers, partners, directors, employees and anyone advising on the firm's behalf (includes clerical). Associated person excludes clerical/ministerial staff. Independent contractors are IARs supervised by the firm.

terms.def: Any person who, for compensation, is in the business of advising others about securities or issuing analyses or reports about securities.
An individual, corporation, partnership, association, trust, government or political subdivision; the three nonpersons are a minor, a deceased individual and a court-declared incompetent.
Advice about securities + in the business + compensation = investment adviser.
An adviser whose principal business is investment advice and that provides investment supervisory services.
1987 interpretation extending the IA definition to financial planners, pension consultants and sports/entertainment representatives.
Not included in the definition of investment adviser; only antifraud provisions apply.
Defined as an investment adviser but not required to register.
Adviser solely under SEC jurisdiction (NSMIA 1996), excluded from the USA definition; registers only with the SEC and notice files with states.
Lawyer, accountant, teacher, engineer whose advice is solely incidental to the profession and who charges no separate fee.
A program charging one fee not based on transactions for advisory services plus execution; the BD exclusion is lost.
Compensation to a broker-dealer or salesperson in excess of what is paid for brokerage alone — a clearly definable charge for advice.
State exemption for an adviser with no place of business in the state and five or fewer retail clients there in the preceding 12 months.
No state registration needed for existing nonresident clients temporarily in the state; 30 days to register if a client becomes a resident.
Banks, trust companies, S&Ls, insurance companies, investment companies, employee benefit plans with at least $1 million, and government agencies.
A noninstitutional client; any individual, trust or estate.
An issuer that would be an investment company but for Section 3(c)(1) (≤100 accredited investors) or 3(c)(7) (qualified purchasers) of the Investment Company Act.
Exemption from SEC registration for advisers solely to private funds with less than $150 million in U.S. AUM.
Investor with at least $5 million in investments (individual) or generally $25 million (entity); permitted in 3(c)(7) funds.
At least $1.1 million in AUM with the adviser, or net worth over $2.2 million excluding the primary residence.
Exempt private fund or VC adviser that still files certain Form ADV Part 1 items through IARD; no Part 2.
Report filed by SEC-registered advisers managing private funds with at least $150 million in private fund AUM.
Non-U.S. adviser with no U.S. office, fewer than 15 U.S. clients/investors, under $25 million U.S. AUM, not holding itself out in the U.S.
Private fund with limited leverage, no redemption rights, holding itself out as VC, not registered under the 1940 Act; its adviser is exempt with unlimited AUM.
National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996 — advisers register with the SEC or the states, not both.
The measure determining SEC vs. state registration; measured on the annual updating amendment.
Form ADV update filed within 90 days after the adviser's fiscal year end.
Investment Adviser Registration Depository — the electronic system for adviser registration, review and public disclosure.
The adviser registration form: Part 1A (all), 1B (state only), 2A (brochure), 2B (brochure supplements).
Power to direct management or policies; presumed at 25% or more of voting securities or partnership capital.
A federal covered adviser's filing of SEC documents and fees with a state in lieu of registration.
Appoints the Administrator as attorney to receive noncriminal securities-related legal process; filed once, permanent.
Form used to withdraw an adviser's registration; SEC 60-day tail, state 30 days effective with 1-year jurisdiction.
More than $500 (USA) or more than $1,200 (federal), six months or more in advance.
Bond from an insurer guaranteeing payment to an injured party when a securities professional causes damage or fails to perform.
The executive office from which the adviser's officers, partners or managers direct, control and coordinate its activities.
Assets minus liabilities, excluding goodwill, intangibles, personal items, and loans to officers or partners.
Trading on the anticipated short-run effect of a recommendation before it is disseminated.
The person designated to administer the adviser's written compliance policies; disclosed on Form ADV.
Any officer, partner, director, employee or other person advising on the adviser's behalf under its supervision (includes clerical staff).

terms.term: Person associated with an investment adviser
terms.def: Partners, officers, directors, control persons and employees of an adviser, excluding those with clerical or ministerial functions.
